citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed Riemann surface and $m\ge1$. Give $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ its usual complex charts of elementary symmetric coordinates in disjoint support disks. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to X$ be the quotient and $p_i:\Sigma^m\to\Sigma$ its factor projections. For $i<j$ let $\Delta_{ij}=\{z_i=z_j\}$, and put $R=\sum_{i<j}\Delta_{ij}$, with coefficient one on every pair diagonal, including at their intersections. Then there is a holomorphic line-bundle isomorphism
$$q^*\det_{\mathbb C}(TX)\cong\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^m p_i^*T\Sigma\right)\otimes\mathcal O(R).$$
Under this isomorphism the holomorphic section $\det(dq)$ of
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}\left(\bigotimes_i p_i^*T\Sigma,q^*\det_{\mathbb C}(TX)\right)$$
corresponds to the canonical divisor section of $\mathcal O(R)$. In particular its zero divisor is exactly $R$, even at tuples with three or more equal entries; no transverse-intersection or simple-branch hypothesis is needed for the bundle identity.

Here $\mathcal O(R)$ is constructed by the actual local defining functions in the proof. For a smooth map $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):C\to\Sigma^m$ from a closed oriented surface with supplied finite smooth triangle data, the identity implies the degree formula
$$\deg\bigl((qF)^*\det(TX)\bigr)=\sum_i\deg(f_i^*T\Sigma)+\sum_{i<j}\deg\bigl((f_i,f_j)^*\mathcal O(\Delta)\bigr),$$
where $\Delta\subset\Sigma\times\Sigma$ is the ordinary diagonal. Degree means the finite face-winding degree of a complex line bundle. Whenever a pulled-back diagonal section has finitely many isolated zeros, its degree is the sum of their signed local winding indices; at a transverse coincidence this is the sign of $d(f_i-f_j)$ in an oriented surface coordinate. Degrees remain defined if two maps coincide identically.

For $m=1$ the empty divisor has its trivial line and constant section one; $q$ is the identity. For $m=0$ all determinants and tensor products over the one-point symmetric product are trivial and the degree formula is zero. This result does not identify the diagonal class in surface cohomology, compute a sphere's degree, prove a Maslov/domain formula, or realize arbitrary Whitney classes by incidence covers.

Assume countable choice. Retain the compact target, totally real boundary submanifolds, fixed path $J_t$ and exact product generator charts of the smooth relative-homotopy index lemma. A continuous Whitney representative from $x$ to $y$ is a continuous disk map with two specified boundary points mapped to $x,y$ and its two boundary arcs mapped into $L_0,L_1$. Equivalence means an actual continuous relative homotopy fixing those points and preserving the two boundary conditions.

Every such class has a smooth fixed-end strip representative, constant on full tails. If two smooth fixed-end representatives are continuously relatively homotopic, there is a smooth relative homotopy between them with one common pair of constant tails and the same fixed endpoints. Consequently the quotient of smooth fixed-end representatives by those smooth homotopies identifies with the continuous Whitney-class set. The actual real Fredholm index of its fixed-end Cauchy–Riemann-symbol linearization therefore defines an integer $\mu(\phi)$ on every continuous Whitney class; it agrees with the actual index of each smooth fixed-end model, is additive under class concatenation, is zero on the constant class, and changes sign under reversal.

For an actual smooth finite-energy holomorphic strip with uniform generator ends, its actual Fredholm index equals this index of its continuously compactified Whitney class.

This proves a continuous-class index using genuine representatives and relative homotopies. It does not identify that integer with a domain Euler measure, corner multiplicities or a first-Chern pairing; no nonlinear moduli counts or their regularity are asserted.

Assume countable choice. Let $X$ be a compact smooth manifold with a smooth path $J_t$ of almost complex structures, and let $L_0,L_1$ be compact submanifolds totally real for $J_0,J_1$, respectively. Suppose their intersection is finite and transverse. At each intersection point choose a target chart in which $L_0=\mathbb R^m$, $L_1=i\mathbb R^m$ and $J_t=i$ for every $t$. Retain those same charts and structures throughout.

A smooth fixed-end representative from $x$ to $y$ is a smooth map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to X$ with boundary on $L_0,L_1$, identically $x$ on one full negative tail and identically $y$ on one full positive tail. Its covariant Cauchy–Riemann linearization on fixed-end $H^1\to L^2$ spaces is Fredholm. Its real index is independent of the chosen smooth connection and of the representative under any smooth relative homotopy $H(h,s,t)$ with those boundary conditions, fixed endpoints, and one common pair of constant tails for all $h\in[0,1]$.

These indices add under concatenating two such representatives at their common endpoint, are zero for a constant representative, and change sign when $u(s,t)$ is replaced by $u(-s,t)$. Thus they define an integer index on smooth fixed-end representatives modulo the stated smooth relative homotopies, with concatenation and reversal laws. This result includes nonholomorphic representatives. It does not assume that a nonlinear moduli space exists or is regular.

A further relative smoothing and end-flattening argument is required to identify this smooth quotient with a Whitney-class set defined initially by arbitrary continuous disk maps and continuous relative homotopies. No such identification, domain Euler formula, or arbitrary-class representativity theorem is asserted here.

Assume Countable Choice. Consider an actual smooth complex rank-$m$ strip bundle, totally real horizontal boundary subbundles, specified end frames identifying these subbundles with $\mathbb R^m,i\mathbb R^m$, and a smooth real first-order operator with Cauchy–Riemann symbol and exact expression $\partial_s+i\partial_t$ in those frames outside a compact set. Its index means the real Fredholm index before source translation, on fixed-end $H^{q+1}\to H^q$ spaces, for an integer $q\ge0$.

Take a compact strip rectangle $Q$ containing the nonconstant part. Complete the horizontal boundary subbundles to a totally real loop along $\partial Q$ using the vertical end caps
$$L_\pm(t)=\tau_\pm e^{i\pi\rho(t)/2}\mathbb R^m,$$
where $\rho:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ is smooth, zero near zero, one near one, and increases from zero to one. The boundary orientation is that induced by $ds\wedge dt$. In any smooth global complex frame on $Q$, a local real basis $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ of this loop defines
$$\zeta=\frac{(\det_{\mathbb C}(v_1,\ldots,v_m))^2}{|\det_{\mathbb C}(v_1,\ldots,v_m)|^2}\in S^1.$$
These local expressions agree on overlaps. Its integer winding $M$ is independent of real bases, global complex frame, sufficiently large rectangle, and cap cutoff $\rho$, and
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}P=M.$$
The equality also holds with smooth two-sided weights below the end spectral gap $\pi/2$. This specifies actual caps and signs, rather than defining an unexplained topological index.

The following finite-dimensional excision and model calculations hold with the same squared determinant convention.

* Direct sums add $M$. Gluing two such strip problems with matching product end frames and operators exactly constant near the cut adds their actual real indices. This is a statement about the glued linear boundary problem.
* On a rectangle with finitely many disjoint round interior disks removed, suppose a continuous totally real subbundle in a trivial complex bundle is defined on the remaining compact surface. Then the determinant winding along the outer boundary is the sum of its windings along the positively counterclockwise hole circles. It suffices that the bundle be smooth near the boundary circles; for a smooth bundle the local windings can be computed by the following models.
* For the symmetric-coordinate map $q(z_1,z_2)=(z_1+z_2,z_1z_2)$, transport the two real lines generated by the same nonzero constant $v\in\mathbb C$ along $z_1=-\sqrt w,z_2=\sqrt w$, $w$ traversing a small counterclockwise circle. Their image under $dq$ has squared determinant winding $+1$. More generally an order-$r$ source-cover model consisting of the $r$ roots of $w$, with the same constant source vector on each sheet and elementary symmetric target coordinates, has winding $r-1$.
* A scalar target map $f(z)=z^{r+1}$, on a sheet unbranched over the parameter disk, sends a nonzero constant real direction to a line of squared phase winding $2r$ along a positive source circle.
* For two graph branches $(z,Az),(z,Bz)$ in $\mathbb C\times\mathbb C$, with $A,B:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ real linear invertible and $A-B$ invertible, choose source directions $A^{-1}v,B^{-1}v$ for a fixed nonzero $v\in\mathbb C$. Push their target directions to the symmetric coordinates of $Az,Bz$. The resulting two-plane has squared determinant winding $2\operatorname{sign}\det_{\mathbb R}(A-B)$. This sign equals the oriented intersection sign of the two graph sheets, both oriented by their $z$ coordinate and the product oriented by base then target.
* A scalar source direction winding $k$ on an otherwise nonsingular sheet contributes $2k$ to the squared determinant winding. Extra fixed nonzero product directions change none of these local contributions.

These assertions do not identify the domain Euler measure or corner multiplicities of an arbitrary Whitney class. In particular, no representativity theorem, collapsed-tube calculation, corner rounding formula, or branched-cover Euler identity is included.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E\to\overline{\mathbb D}$ be a smooth complex vector bundle of rank $m\ge1$, with complex multiplication $J$, and let $F\subset E|_{\partial\mathbb D}$ be a smooth oriented totally real real subbundle of rank $m$. Let $P$ be a smooth real-linear first-order operator on sections with exact Cauchy–Riemann symbol: for real smooth $h$ and smooth $\xi$,
$$P(h\xi)=hP\xi+h_x\xi+h_yJ\xi.$$
Use smooth positive definite metrics and finite smooth charts to define $H^r(E)$ by weak derivatives for integers $r\ge1$. Let $X_0$ be the $H^1$ closure of smooth sections with boundary values in $F$, and put $X_q=H^{q+1}(E)\cap X_0$, $Y_q=H^q(E)$ for integers $q\ge0$. Only the zeroth boundary condition is imposed.

There is a smooth global complex frame of $E$ and an integer $k$ in which the boundary condition is
$$F(e^{it})=e^{ikt}\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R^{m-1}$$
and the actual operator is $\partial_x+i\partial_y+B$ with smooth real-linear zeroth-order coefficient $B$. Equivalently, before this reduction, if $C(t)$ is the complex matrix whose columns are any smooth periodic oriented real frame of $F$ in any global complex frame, then
$$k=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{(\det C)'(t)}{\det C(t)}\,dt.$$
Such frames exist, and this integer is independent of both choices.

Every actual realization $P_q:X_q\to Y_q$ is bounded Fredholm with real index $m+2k$. Its kernel is the same set as the $H^1$ kernel, its range is $Y_q\cap\operatorname{Ran}P_0$, and inclusion in $L^2$ identifies its real cokernel with that of $P_0$. For $\xi\in X_0$ and $P\xi=f\in H^q$,
$$\|\xi\|_{H^{q+1}}\le C_q(\|f\|_{H^q}+\|\xi\|_{H^1}).$$
The inverse of $P_0$ from its $H^1$ kernel complement to its closed range is bounded, and its restriction gives a bounded range inverse $H^q\cap\operatorname{Ran}P_0\to X_q$. The statement applies to an actual geometric linearization along a smooth disk with oriented totally real boundary. It does not assert its surjectivity, compute a Heegaard domain formula, or supply a puncture or gluing theorem.

derivations.claim: Lift $R$ to the plane and write it as $c+[-a,a]+i[-b,b]$ with $a,b>0$ and side lengths less than $n$. Quotient this rectangle by $z\mapsto-z$ and use $w=z^2$ as its actual interior complex coordinate. This quotient is a disk: each radial ray in the $w$ plane has an interval from zero to its boundary, whose radial length is the square of the rectangle's radial length at half the angle. Its boundary consists of two arcs meeting at the two images of opposite corners; the map is smooth up to these arcs and their corners. Define the active roots to be $c+z,c-z$ modulo the torus periods and retain all inactive coordinates of $x$. The symmetric map is smooth at $w=0$ because its two active elementary symmetric coordinates are $2c,c^2-w$. Along the horizontal boundary arc the two roots lie on their original alpha circles; along the vertical arc they lie on their beta circles. Positive source-boundary orientation traverses the horizontal arc from the northeast/southwest tuple $x$ to the northwest/southeast tuple $y$. This constructs the stated continuous Whitney disk. [F4, given, construct, algebra]

Now let the row annulus be $i\le\operatorname{Im}z\le i+1$ modulo $n$, and put $c_y=i+1/2$ and $r=e^{-\pi/n}$. On $A=\{r\le|\zeta|\le r^{-1}\}$ define $$f(\zeta)=c_x+ic_y+\frac{n}{2\pi i}\log\zeta\pmod{n\mathbb Z+in\mathbb Z}.$$ Changing a logarithm adds $n$, so this is well defined and is a biholomorphism of the annulus interior onto the open row annulus. The map $p(\zeta)=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$ has the two simple branch points $\pm1$ and maps $A$ properly with degree two onto the closed ellipse with semiaxes $r+r^{-1}$ and $r^{-1}-r$. Indeed both boundary circles have that same ellipse as image, with reciprocal boundary points paired, and every fiber solves $\zeta^2-p\zeta+1=0$; the pair above $p=0$ lies inside $A$, so the two-root count is constant throughout the ellipse interior. No interior root can escape across its boundary without its image reaching that ellipse. The exterior contains no fiber in $A$, since the count is zero near infinity and its only possible crossing locus is the ellipse. [given, construct, algebra]

Its coordinate incidence surface is precisely the lifted rectangle, with one root above every generic point of its interior and none above its exterior; the inactive roots contribute constant maps only. Thus its point-divisor degrees are exactly the region chain $R$. No inactive root meets the rectangle: none lies on its boundary by the one-point-per-row/column condition, and none lies inside by the empty-state-interior hypothesis. Hence its only repeated tuple is the active exchange at $w=0$. In a local determinant frame the squared wedge section $\sigma$ from $V=1$ is a nonzero constant times $w$ there, by [F1]; it has no other zero. It follows that the boundary winding of $\sigma$ in any complex disk frame is $1$. This last equality is the finite argument principle for a line section: remove a small disk about its one zero, trivialize on finitely many patches of the remaining annulus, and cancel their common-edge argument changes, leaving the local winding $1$. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Send this ellipse to a round disk by its positive diagonal real affine map. To each point of that disk assign the unordered pair of values $f(\zeta),f(\zeta^{-1})$ above it, and keep the remaining $n-2$ coordinates of $x$ fixed. It is an actual smooth symmetric map, including at the two branch points: in local coordinates its roots are exchanged by a holomorphic involution, and their elementary symmetric coefficients are holomorphic functions of $p$ before the real affine change. On the boundary one root lies on each of the two consecutive alpha circles. If the two required generator coordinates on the upper and lower circles have real lifts $x_u,x_l$, choose $c_x=(x_u+x_l)/2$ and $\theta=\pi(x_u-x_l)/n$. The boundary pair $\zeta=r e^{i\theta},\zeta^{-1}=r^{-1}e^{-i\theta}$ then gives exactly these generator entries. Taking its image point as the marked disk node makes this an actual based disk at $x$. The other roots lie on different alpha circles, hence outside the closed row annulus. The incidence map $f$ has degree one over that annulus and zero elsewhere, so its domain is the asserted unit annulus. [step 1.2, construct, algebra]

Relate this section to the actual strip caps, rather than identifying it with a compact disk problem with a single boundary condition. On the alpha boundary, the normalized squared determinant of the physical plane equals that of $\sigma$. On the beta boundary it equals $(-1)^n$ times that value, because each real coordinate vector is replaced by $iV$. At each marked corner all roots are distinct. Use its ordered flat product frame and the cap $e^{i\pi t/2}\mathbb R^n$, $0\le t\le1$. Its squared determinant is $e^{in\pi t}$ times the alpha value. Choose a continuous scalar function $t$ on the disk core, equal to $0$ on the alpha arc, $1$ on the beta arc, and to the indicated cap parameter on the two inserted constant corner collars. Such a function is obtained by interpolation in a rectangle model of the punctured disk; the collars are disjoint. Consequently the completed physical phase is the boundary phase of $\sigma$ multiplied by $e^{in\pi t}$. The second factor extends over the core, so has winding zero. The first has winding $1$ by step 2.1. Corner flattening in the two product charts by a real scalar cutoff preserves both planes, and changes this calculation only by a relative homotopy. [F2] therefore gives actual fixed-end index $1$, also for every allowed homotopic target complex structure. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

There are no coincidences with inactive coordinates. Equality of the two active values of $f$ would force their logarithmic arguments to differ by a torus period; their imaginary coordinates lie in an interval of length $1<n$, so only the horizontal period can occur. Therefore $\zeta^2=1$, precisely the two branch points. Since $df$ is nonzero there, [F1]'s section $\sigma$ has one positive simple zero at each, and no others. On the entire physical boundary its normalized value is the squared real tangent determinant for $L_\alpha$, since $V=1$ is tangent to every alpha circle. The finite line-section argument of step 2.1 and [F3] give boundary Maslov index $2$. A column annulus is obtained by the orientation-preserving torus rotation $z\mapsto iz$ from the same construction with the corresponding generator. Now $V=i$ is tangent to every beta circle; the constant factor $i^n$ in its wedge has no winding, so its boundary Maslov index is again $2$. This rotation is used only for a one-system based disk and does not exchange the alpha/beta conditions in the rectangle assertion. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

Flatten either based disk near its node in a product chart by a real scalar cutoff, which preserves its one real boundary plane. Insert this disk on the corresponding side of the constant strip at $x$: glue its constant node collar to a small constant boundary interval of that strip, retaining both outer marked strip ends. A smooth rounded planar source for this glued disk is obtained by connecting their two collar rectangles and rounding their finitely many corners; both maps are constant on the joining rectangles. It is a continuous Whitney representative; the relative smoothing and fixed-end construction in [F2] supplies an actual smooth model. The completed determinant phase of its boundary is the constant strip's completed phase with the based disk's physical boundary phase inserted. The two joining constant intervals have identical frames, and their argument changes cancel; hence its winding is $0+2=2$. This directly proves its actual strip index without subtracting a compact disk's $n$-dimensional constant kernel. Domain degrees add by local winding and the inserted disk has its computed unit annulus domain. Finally [F2]'s actual class concatenation and reversal give all the stated sums and negative domains. No nonlinear holomorphic count or moduli regularity entered any step. [F2, F3, step 3.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra] ∎

citations.quote: Let $G$ be a toroidal grid of grid number $n$ representing one oriented knot, and let $M_{\mathbb O}$, $M_{\mathbb X}$, and $A_G$ be the functions defined from its finite point sets and the pair-counting function $J$. Then $M_{\mathbb O}$ and $M_{\mathbb X}$ are integer-valued, and every rectangle $r$ from a grid state $\mathbf x$ to a grid state $\mathbf y$ satisfies $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$ and $M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb X}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. Consequently $A_G$ is integer-valued and $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Use a size-$n\ge2$ toroidal grid, its flat oriented torus $T=\mathbb R^2/(n\mathbb Z)^2$, horizontal alpha circles and vertical beta circles, and $X=\operatorname{Sym}^n(T)$. At each generator use the actual flat product chart with alpha plane $\mathbb R^n$ and beta plane $i\mathbb R^n$. The path of target almost complex structures may be any homotopy of the standard complex structure compatible with these boundary planes and fixed product ends as in the relative-index suppliers.

For each embedded grid rectangle $R$ from $x$ to $y$, with $x$ at its northeast and southwest corners and with no other point of $x$ in its interior, there is an actual continuous Whitney class $r_R:x\to y$ whose domain is exactly $R$ and whose actual fixed-end Fredholm index is $1$. Markings inside $R$ are unrestricted.

For every generator $x$ and every closed band between consecutive horizontal grid circles there is an actual based disk on $L_\alpha$, based at $x$, with domain that unit row annulus and boundary Maslov index $2$. Likewise every consecutive column annulus is the domain of an actual based disk on $L_\beta$ with boundary Maslov index $2$. Inserting either disk on the corresponding boundary of the constant Whitney class at $x$ gives a class $x\to x$ of actual fixed-end index $2$. Reversals give the negative domains and negative indices, and finite concatenations are actual classes with additive domains and indices.

All these assertions construct classes and compute their linearized indices. They do not count holomorphic representatives, prove moduli regularity, or identify absolute gradings or an analytic invariant.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented Riemann surface with an actual finite oriented polygon as in the sphere-index theorem, $m\ge1$, and put $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$. Let $\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta$ be two disjoint-within-system smooth curve families of size $m$, transverse to each other, with product tori $L_\alpha,L_\beta$. Give two smooth fixed-end Whitney disk models $u,v$ from the same generator $x$ to the same generator $y$, constant near their two marked boundary corners, with their actual fixed product end data. Use the auxiliary complex-structure homotopies and actual relative-index realizations specified in the relative Whitney index theorem. Domain coefficients mean the integer relative degrees of the point-divisor lines, not a holomorphic representative assumption.

For any such pair, $D(u)-D(v)$ has boundary a sum of full attaching circles. The coefficient on each oriented circle is the angular winding difference of the corresponding labelled boundary paths, with their source-boundary signs. In particular, if $D(u)=D(v)$ as region chains, their boundary paths on each labelled alpha circle are homotopic relative their endpoints, and likewise on each labelled beta circle. After these boundary homotopies the difference of their smooth relative classes is represented by a sphere $A$ with $n_z(A)=0$. Consequently
$$\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}(u)=\operatorname{ind}_{\mathbb R}(v),$$
before source translation, on all the stated higher Sobolev and allowed smooth weighted realizations. Thus actual Fredholm index is well defined on the set of REALIZED Whitney domains, including classes with positive, zero or negative marked multiplicities. No assertion that every integer region chain is realized is made.

The analogous statement holds for two smooth disks based at the same point of a single product torus $L_\gamma$, with equal one-system domains: their boundary loops are based homotopic, and their boundary Maslov indices and compact-disk Fredholm indices agree. Their fixed-node indices also agree whenever that bounded point-trace realization is used. The finite polygon hypothesis is supplied for the original embedded balanced $S^3$ data by the broad-input application in the sphere-index theorem. No full formula $e(D)+n_x(D)+n_y(D)$, normalized relative or absolute grading, invariance, or arbitrary-domain representativity is included.

derivations.claim: Label the grid rows and columns cyclically by $0,\ldots,n-1$. A state is its permutation of columns along the rows. Any two permutations are joined by finitely many swaps of consecutive rows: move the column wanted in row zero there by successive adjacent swaps, then do the same in row one without changing row zero, and continue. At each swap use the row band between those consecutive circles and the positively directed column interval from the lower point's column to the upper point's column. Its width is strictly between zero and $n$ because state columns are distinct. Its southwest and northeast corners are the two old points, so it is an oriented rectangle from the old state to the swapped state. Its height is one row band, with no other state points inside. Thus [F2] supplies a finite concatenation $r:x\to y$ of actual empty-state rectangles, with actual domain $D_0$ and additive index. This proves connectivity by actual represented classes, not by declaring arbitrary region chains realizable. [F2, given, construct, algebra]

Choose an actual smooth model for $\phi$ by [F4], and for $r$ by [F2]. Put $P=D(\phi)-D_0$. By [F3], $\partial P$ is a sum of whole alpha and beta circles. Write $P_{ij}$ for the coefficient on the cell in row band $i$ and column band $j$. The jump across a vertical edge is independent of its row, because it is the coefficient of one whole beta circle. Thus $$P_{ij}-P_{i,j-1}=P_{0j}-P_{0,j-1}$$ for every cyclic pair of neighboring columns. Telescoping from column zero gives $$P_{ij}=a_i+b_j,\qquad a_i=P_{i0},\quad b_j=P_{0j}-P_{00}.$$ This includes the wraparound edges, since the original coefficients are cyclic. It is an explicit integer identity, requiring neither a homology-basis assertion nor realization of a formal periodic chain. Hence $P$ is the sum of $a_i$ times the unit row annulus $i$ and $b_j$ times the unit column annulus $j$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

At the final generator $y$ append the actual row and column loop classes of [F2], with these integer multiplicities, using reversals for negative integers and no factor for zero. There are finitely many factors. This produces an actual class $r':x\to y$ with domain $D_0+P=D(\phi)$. Its index is the sum of the rectangle indices plus $2\sum_i a_i+2\sum_j b_j$. Apply [F3] to actual smooth models of $r'$ and $\phi$: their domains are equal, so their actual indices are equal. No claim that their relative homotopy classes coincide is needed; a zero-domain sphere difference has zero index by that supplier. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

For an actual class $q:v\to w$ put $$H(q)=M_O(v)-M_O(w)+2\sum_i n_{O_i}(q).$$ Domain degrees add under concatenation, so $H$ adds by cancellation of the intermediate $M_O$ values, and it negates under reversal. On every rectangle in step1.1 it equals $1$ by [F1]. On each annulus loop it equals $2$, because the endpoint values agree and exactly one $O$ mark lies in that unit band. Therefore $H(r')$ equals the actual index sum in step3.1. Since $r'$ and $\phi$ have the same endpoints and domain, $H(\phi)=H(r')=\mu(\phi)$, proving the full Maslov identity. The nonunique decomposition obtained by adding a constant to all $a_i$ and subtracting it from all $b_j$ gives the same sum, since there are $n$ rows and $n$ columns; no consistency obstruction is hidden in the chosen decomposition. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

The rectangle formulas for $P=O,X$ in [F1] give $$A_G(v)-A_G(w)=n_X(R)-n_O(R).$$ This relation adds along the actual rectangle path. A unit row or column loop has one $X$ and one $O$, so both sides of the claimed Alexander relation vanish on that loop and on its reversal. It consequently holds on the actual concatenation $r'$. Equal endpoints and equal domains transfer it to $\phi$ exactly as in step4.1. Negative, zero and positive domain coefficients all obey these integer identities. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

For an actual holomorphic strip [F4] identifies its actual linearized index with the class index just computed. If its index is one, the Maslov identity rearranges to $$M_O(y)-2\sum_i n_{O_i}=M_O(x)-1.$$ With the prescribed variable degrees this is precisely the Maslov degree of its weighted output. The Alexander identity likewise gives $$A_G(y)-\sum_i n_{O_i}=A_G(x)-\sum_i n_{X_i}.$$ Nonnegativity of the actual marked multiplicities therefore gives filtration preservation and the stated exact drop, without imposing $n_X=0$. No existence, compactification, count cancellation or grading normalization independent of the grid was used to obtain these relative formulas; those remain separate obligations.
